chapterTitle: A framework for system design interviews

quests.d: What the interviewer is really grading, the red flags, the 4-step clock, and the dos and don'ts
quests.winTitle: You know the rules of the game
quests.goal: Your win today: explain what a system design interview tests, name the three red flags, recite the four steps with their minute ranges, and list the core dos and don'ts.
quests.bookSections: Chapter opening (what the interview simulates and what is assessed, red flags); the 45-minute time allocation; Dos and Don'ts lists at the end of the chapter

stages.title: Two Coworkers, One Whiteboard
stages.sub: What the interview is really simulating
stages.teaches: Book's framing in our words: the session imitates two colleagues working together on a vague problem and arriving at a workable answer. You get asked to 'design' products that took hundreds or thousands of engineers years to build, so nobody expects a finished system in under an hour. There's no single right answer, and the final diagram matters less than how you got there. What the interviewer writes down (the 'signal'): (1) technical design skill, (2) collaboration, (3) working under pressure, (4) resolving ambiguity (turning a fuzzy prompt into a concrete scope), (5) asking good questions. Define 'signal' inline: the evidence an interviewer records to justify hire or no-hire.
stages.interaction: Signal radar. On screen: an empty 5-spoke radar chart (Design skill, Collaboration, Under pressure, Ambiguity, Good questions) and a stack of 7 short candidate-behaviour cards, one at a time. For each card the learner taps the spoke it gives evidence for; correct taps grow that spoke and show a one-line reason; wrong taps shake and show the right spoke. Cards (answer): 'Asks how many daily users before drawing anything' → Good questions; 'Interviewer pushes back on SQL; candidate asks what worries them and adjusts' → Collaboration; 'Says the prompt could mean a web app or a mobile app, picks one aloud and notes it' → Ambiguity; 'Explains why a cache in front of the DB cuts read latency' → Design skill; 'At minute 30 a new requirement lands; candidate re-plans calmly instead of freezing' → Under pressure; 'Proposes two storage options and their trade-offs' → Design skill; 'Checks in: does this level of detail work for you?' → Collaboration. When all 7 are placed, the radar is full and a caption reads: the diagram is the by-product; the radar is what gets graded.
stages.check: Quiz: 'In a 45-minute session, what is the interviewer mainly trying to learn?' Options: A finished, production-ready design / How you reason, collaborate and handle ambiguity on the way to a design (correct) / Whether you know the company's real architecture / How many technologies you can name.

stages.title: Red Flag Detector
stages.teaches: The book names three red flags. Over-engineering: loving design purity and ignoring trade-offs; many engineers don't see how the costs of an over-built system pile up over time, and companies pay heavily for it. Narrow-mindedness: locking onto one idea and not considering alternatives. Stubbornness: refusing to adjust when the interviewer raises a valid concern. Contrast with healthy behaviour that looks similar: defending a choice with reasons and then updating when new facts appear is good, not stubborn; choosing a simple design for a small scale is good, not narrow.
stages.interaction: Spot-the-flag transcript. On screen: a chat transcript (10 lines) of a candidate designing a URL shortener for a small internal tool (1,000 users). The learner taps any line they think is a red flag, then picks which of the three flags it is from a mini-menu. Hidden flags (3): candidate proposes multi-region active-active replication with a custom consensus layer for 1,000 internal users (over-engineering); interviewer asks 'could a relational DB work here?' and candidate says 'NoSQL is always better, let's move on' (narrow-mindedness); interviewer says the 7-character code space seems too small for their numbers and candidate repeats the same plan without addressing it (stubbornness). Decoys (2) that should NOT be flagged: candidate says 'I'd start with a single database since we're tiny, and shard later if needed' (simple is fine); candidate defends a choice with a reason, then says 'good point, given that, I'd switch to X' (healthy). Score: +XP per correct flag and type, a heart lost for flagging a decoy, with an explanation either way.
stages.check: Quiz: 'The interviewer questions your cache choice. You think you're right. Best move?' Options: Repeat your plan more firmly / Drop the cache immediately to please them / Explain your reasoning, ask what concern they have, and adjust if their point holds (correct) / Change topic to something you know better.

stages.title: Budget the 45 Minutes
stages.sub: The four steps and their clocks
stages.teaches: The framework's four steps in order: 1) understand the problem and set the design scope, 2) propose a high-level design and get buy-in, 3) deep dive into the design, 4) wrap up. Book's rough guide for a 45-minute session: Step 1 scope 3–10 min · Step 2 high-level design + buy-in 10–15 min · Step 3 deep dive 10–25 min · Step 4 wrap-up 3–5 min (book's rough guide for a 45-minute session). The ranges don't add up neatly on purpose: minimums sum to 26 min, maximums to 55, so you flex depending on the problem and the interviewer. The deep dive has the widest range (10–25) and is where the remaining time goes. Spending too long on any one step starves the next.
stages.interaction: Two parts. (a) Slider budget: four sliders (one per step) and a 45-minute bar that fills as you drag. The learner must hit exactly 45 with each step inside its book range; out-of-range sliders turn red and show the range. Any valid split passes (example: 7 / 13 / 21 / 4). (b) Predict-then-watch: show 'Candidate Sam' with a split of 20 / 15 / 7 / 3. Learner predicts what goes wrong: 'Ran out of time for the deep dive, so the interviewer never saw depth' (correct) vs 'The interviewer was impressed by thoroughness' vs 'Nothing, any split is fine'. Then animate the 45-minute bar: step 1 overruns into red, the deep dive gets squeezed to 7 minutes and a toast says 'interviewer: we're out of time; I'd hoped to see how you'd scale the feed'.
stages.check: Quiz: 'Which step has the widest time range in the book's guide?' Options: Scoping / High-level design / Deep dive, 10–25 min (correct) / Wrap-up.

stages.title: Dos & Don'ts Sorter
stages.sub: The chapter's checklist, in your own hands
stages.teaches: Dos (paraphrased): ask for clarification, never treat your own assumption as fact; understand the requirements; remember there is no single best answer (a young startup and a company with millions of users need different designs); think out loud so the interviewer can follow; offer more than one approach when you can; once the blueprint is agreed, go into detail on each component, most critical first; bounce ideas off the interviewer like a teammate; don't give up. Don'ts: don't arrive unprepared for the common questions; don't jump into a solution before clarifying requirements and assumptions; don't go deep on one component at the start, give the high-level picture first; if stuck, don't be shy about asking for a hint; don't think in silence; don't treat the interview as finished once the design is on the board, you're done when the interviewer says so, and ask for feedback early and often.
stages.interaction: Sort cards. 12 paraphrased behaviour cards drop one at a time; the learner swipes/taps each into DO or DON'T. Cards: Ask what scale to plan for (DO) · Assume it's mobile-only without saying so (DON'T) · Offer two storage options and compare them (DO) · Spend minute 3 designing the database index layout (DON'T) · Ask for a hint after being stuck for a while (DO) · Go quiet for 4 minutes to think (DON'T) · Say 'I think we're done' after drawing the boxes (DON'T) · Ask 'does this direction make sense to you?' (DO) · Detail the most critical component first (DO) · Assume there's one textbook answer you must find (DON'T) · Practise common prompts beforehand (DO) · Give up when a curveball lands (DON'T). Wrong sorts cost a heart and flip the card to show the reason.
stages.check: Quiz: 'You've been stuck on how to keep the feed fresh for two minutes. What do you do?' Options: Keep thinking silently until it comes / Say what you've considered so far and ask for a hint (correct) / Skip it and pretend it's solved / Start over with a new design.

stages.title: Boss: The Interviewer's Notebook
stages.teaches: Applying the rules to concrete moments, including the subtle cases where a good behaviour looks like a bad one.
stages.interaction: Q.boss() with fixed choices: 'Strong signal', 'Red flag', 'Neutral / depends'. Scenarios (answer, why): 1) Candidate asks 'are we a startup or a big company?' → Strong signal (scale and context change the design). 2) For a 10-user prototype, candidate adds Kafka, Kubernetes and three caches → Red flag (over-engineering). 3) Interviewer hints about hot keys; candidate says 'interesting, here's how that changes my sharding' → Strong signal (collaboration under pressure). 4) Candidate draws for 12 minutes without speaking → Red flag (thinking in silence). 5) Candidate picks a relational DB and gives a one-line reason → Strong signal (decisive with a trade-off). 6) Candidate says 'my design has no weaknesses' in the wrap-up → Red flag (book: never call it perfect). 7) Candidate asks the interviewer for feedback mid-design → Strong signal. Name: '📓 The Silent Scorer'.
stages.check: Boss round passes with at most 2 wrong; outro: 'Interviewers write down behaviour, not boxes.'

stages.title: Say It Like a Senior
stages.teaches: Being able to state your game plan out loud is itself a signal; some candidates say it at the start of the session.
stages.interaction: Q.drill(): prompt 'A friend asks how you'll approach tomorrow's system design round. Explain your plan in a few sentences.' Model answer (our words): 'I treat it as a design session with a colleague, not a quiz. First 5 to 10 minutes I ask questions and pin down scope and assumptions. Then about 10 to 15 minutes on a high-level box diagram, checking it with the interviewer. Most of the remaining time goes to a deep dive on the parts they care about, most critical first. I keep the last few minutes to flag bottlenecks and what I'd improve. Throughout, I think out loud, offer options with trade-offs, and avoid over-engineering.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: I named all four steps in order · I gave rough minute budgets · I mentioned at least two dos (clarify, think out loud, options, ask for hints) · I mentioned a red flag to avoid.

caveats: The minute ranges are the book's rough guide for a 45-minute slot. Many companies run 45–60 minutes, and some use different shapes (for example, a written requirements doc first). Use the ranges as proportions, not a stopwatch.
The book lists the three red flags; real rubrics vary by company and level. Senior candidates are usually expected to drive the conversation themselves, not wait for prompts.
'Never give up' and 'ask for hints' don't conflict: asking for a hint after trying is fine; a long silent stall is what hurts.

The System Design Primer: how to approach a system design interview question

quests.d: Step 1: turn a vague prompt into a scoped problem with clarifying questions and written-down assumptions
quests.goal: Your win today: in the first 3–10 minutes, ask the questions that matter, write down your assumptions, and lock the scope of 'design a news feed' with the book's numbers.
quests.bookSections: Step 1: Understand the problem and establish design scope, including the news feed Q&A example

stages.title: Don't Sprint to the Answer
stages.teaches: Step 1 budget: 3–10 minutes. Answering instantly earns no bonus points; jumping to a solution before understanding the requirements is a big red flag. Engineers tend to rush to a solution because they like hard problems, but a design aimed at the wrong problem is wasted. Slow down, think, and ask questions. Hidden requirements (media types, friend limits, scale) change the design, and finding them late forces expensive rework.
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch race. Two lanes: Candidate A starts drawing boxes at 0:30; Candidate B spends 6 minutes asking questions. The learner predicts who finishes the session with more signal. Animate a shared 45-minute clock: A's diagram grows fast, then at minute 14 the interviewer says 'by the way, posts include video, and users can have 5,000 friends'; A's text-only DB and naive per-read friend lookup get crossed out in red and an 8-minute 'rework' block eats A's deep dive. B's lane shows a steady build and a full deep dive. End card: B wins, with the line 'fast start, slow finish'.
stages.check: Quiz: 'Why is jumping straight into a solution a red flag?' Options: Interviewers like slow candidates / You may design for the wrong problem and burn time on rework, and it shows you skip requirements (correct) / It isn't, speed is always rewarded / Because diagrams are not allowed in step 1.

stages.title: The Question Deck
stages.teaches: Question families the book suggests: (1) Features: what exactly are we building? (2) Users: how many users does the product have? (3) Growth: how fast should it scale, and what scale is expected in 3 months, 6 months, a year? (4) Stack: what is the company's tech stack, and which existing services could we reuse to simplify the design? Good questions change the design; poor ones (UI colours, which programming language the team prefers for no reason) waste minutes.
stages.interaction: Question budget. Prompt on screen: 'Design a news feed.' A deck of 12 question cards; the learner has a 6-minute budget, each question costs 1 minute. High-value cards (in one of the four families) light up a matching family badge when asked: 'Which features matter most?' (Features), 'How many daily active users?' (Users), 'What scale in 6–12 months?' (Growth), 'Any existing services we can reuse, like an auth or notification service?' (Stack), 'Mobile, web, or both?' (Features), 'Can posts contain images or video?' (Features). Low-value cards cost a minute and shave signal: 'What colour is the like button?', 'Should I use Java or Go?', 'Who are your competitors?', 'How many engineers work here?', 'Do you like microservices?', 'Is there a deadline for launch?' (marked 'borderline: fine if time allows'). Win: all four family badges lit within 6 minutes.
stages.check: Quiz: 'Which question best helps you size the system?' Options: What's the brand colour? / How many daily active users, and how fast will that grow? (correct) / Which IDE does the team use? / Is the office remote?

stages.title: Answer or Assume
stages.teaches: When you ask a question, the interviewer either answers it or tells you to make an assumption. Either way, write it down on the whiteboard so both of you can see it and you can refer back. A stated assumption is a decision you own; a silent assumption is a hidden risk. Prefer assumptions that simplify while staying realistic, and say why.
stages.interaction: Assumption ledger. A chat sim: the learner asks 4 questions; for 3 of them the interviewer replies 'What do you think? You decide.' Each time, 3 response options appear: a stated, reasonable assumption ('I'll assume reverse-chronological order to keep it simple; ranking can come later'), a silent assumption (candidate just continues), or a stall ('I can't continue without knowing'). Choosing the stated assumption pins a sticky note to a 'Assumptions' column on a whiteboard panel; choosing silent adds a ghost note that later, in a mini-replay, causes a mismatch with the interviewer ('Wait, I thought this was web only?'). The 4th question gets a real answer, which goes in a 'Requirements' column.
stages.check: Quiz: 'The interviewer says you can choose the feed order. Best response?' Options: Pick one silently / Say 'I'll assume reverse-chronological for simplicity' and write it down (correct) / Refuse to continue until they decide / Design both orderings in full.

stages.title: Lock the News Feed Scope
stages.teaches: The chapter's example Q&A for 'design a news feed' (facts, our wording): platform: both mobile and web; key features: a user can publish a post and can see friends' posts on their news feed page; order: reverse chronological, by assumption, to keep it simple (ranking is a possible extension); friend limit: up to 5,000 friends per user; traffic: 10 million daily active users (DAU); content: posts can include media, both images and videos. What each fact implies: 5,000 friends means one post may need to reach thousands of feeds (fan-out); 10M DAU means a single server is out; video means large files that belong in object storage and a CDN rather than the main DB; reverse-chronological means no ranking service in v1.
stages.interaction: Requirements board. Six empty slots (Platform, Features, Order, Friends, Traffic, Media) and a shuffled pile of answer chips including distractors (e.g., '1,000 friends', '100M DAU', 'text only', 'ranked by ML'). The learner drags the right chip into each slot; each correct placement flips the slot to reveal 'so what?' (the design implication above). Then a calculate-and-check card, clearly labelled 'stretch: not in this chapter, see Ch. 2': 'If each of the 10M DAU opens the feed 10 times a day, about how many feed reads per second?' Learner types a number; accept 1,000–1,300 (10M × 10 / 86,400 ≈ 1,160), with peak at roughly 2× ≈ 2,300.
stages.check: Quiz: 'Which requirement most directly creates the fan-out problem?' Options: Mobile and web / Up to 5,000 friends per user (correct) / Reverse-chronological order / Images in posts.

stages.title: Boss: First Question Wins
stages.teaches: Transfer: the same scoping habit applied to other prompts from later chapters.
stages.interaction: Q.boss() with fixed choices: 'Features', 'Scale & growth', 'Existing stack', 'Not worth asking'. Each scenario shows a prompt and a candidate question; learner tags which family it belongs to, or that it isn't worth asking. Scenarios: 1) Chat app: 'Is it 1-on-1, group, or both?' → Features. 2) URL shortener: 'How many URLs are created per day?' → Scale & growth. 3) Notification system: 'Do we already have a message queue we can use?' → Existing stack. 4) Rate limiter: 'What font do error pages use?' → Not worth asking. 5) Web crawler: 'How many pages per month, and for how many years do we keep them?' → Scale & growth. 6) Search autocomplete: 'Do we need to support multiple languages?' → Features. 7) News feed: 'Can we reuse the company's existing user graph service for friend lists?' → Existing stack. Name: '🌫️ The Fog of Scope'.
stages.check: Pass with at most 2 wrong; outro: 'Every good opening question changes the design.'

stages.title: Say It Like a Senior
stages.teaches: A crisp scoping opener sets the tone for the whole session.
stages.interaction: Q.drill(): prompt 'The interviewer says: "Design a news feed." Say your first 60 seconds.' Model answer (our words): 'Before I draw anything, a few questions. Is this mobile, web, or both? What are the must-have features, posting and viewing friends' posts? Any ordering, or can I assume newest first? How many friends can a user have, and how many daily active users do we expect, now and in a year? Can posts include images and video? And is there existing infrastructure I should reuse? I'll write down whatever we agree, plus any assumptions I make, so we can refer back.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: I asked about features and platform · I asked about scale (DAU, friends) and growth · I asked about media or the existing stack · I said I'd write assumptions down.

caveats: Many interviewers now expect step 1 to end with an explicit list of functional requirements (what it does) and non-functional ones (latency, availability, consistency). The book covers this implicitly; saying both lists out loud is a cheap win.
Some interviewers want back-of-the-envelope numbers in step 1, others in step 2, others never. The book places them in step 2 as a sanity check; ask which they prefer.
The news feed numbers (5,000 friends, 10M DAU) are the book's illustrative example, not real Facebook figures.
The reads-per-second calculation is our extension, not part of Chapter 3.

quests.d: Step 2: sketch a box diagram, sanity-check it, and get the interviewer on board
quests.goal: Your win today: sketch the news feed's two flows (publish and build) as boxes, decide how much API/schema detail to show, and check in with the interviewer before going deeper.
quests.bookSections: Step 2: Propose high-level design and get buy-in, including the news feed publishing and feed-building high-level figures

stages.title: Treat Them Like a Teammate
stages.teaches: Step 2 budget: 10–15 minutes. Goal: an initial blueprint plus agreement from the interviewer. Collaborate: propose the plan, ask for feedback, treat the interviewer as a teammate; many good interviewers like to be involved. Draw box diagrams of the key components. Do rough maths to check the blueprint fits the scale constraints, thinking out loud, and ask whether the interviewer wants estimation before you do it. Walk through a few concrete use cases: it shapes the design and can surface edge cases you haven't thought of.
stages.interaction: Presentation-style chooser. Chat sim at minute 9. Three ways to start step 2, each played out as a short animated exchange after selection: (a) a 10-minute monologue building every detail (interviewer glazes, a 'signal' meter drops, and at minute 19 the interviewer reveals they wanted to focus elsewhere); (b) a 4-minute sketch of the main boxes, then 'Does this look like the right shape before I go deeper?' (interviewer nods and points at fan-out: meter rises) (correct); (c) asking the interviewer to draw the design for you (meter drops: collaboration isn't delegation). Learner can replay all three.
stages.check: Quiz: 'What does buy-in mean in step 2?' Options: The interviewer approves your salary / You and the interviewer agree the blueprint is a sensible base before you go deeper (correct) / You finish the whole design before asking anything / You let the interviewer choose every component.

stages.title: The Box Toolkit
stages.teaches: Typical boxes the book lists for the diagram: clients (mobile/web), APIs, web servers, data stores, cache, CDN, message queue. One line each: client = where requests start; load balancer = spreads traffic across web servers; web servers = handle requests (stateless so you can add more); data store = durable storage; cache = fast copy of hot data in memory; CDN = servers near users that serve static media like images and video; message queue = buffer that lets one part hand work to another asynchronously.
stages.interaction: Match-the-job. Left column: 7 box icons. Right column: 7 job descriptions in plain words, shuffled ('serves video from a server near the user', 'holds hot data in memory so we skip the DB', 'lets the post service hand slow work to workers later', etc.). Learner taps a box then a job to connect them; a correct pair draws a line and the box snaps into a mini whiteboard at the bottom. Wrong pair costs a heart and shows a hint.
stages.check: Quiz: 'Posts include video. Which box serves video quickly to users worldwide?' Options: Message queue / CDN (correct) / Load balancer / Relational database.

stages.title: Two Flows of a Feed
stages.teaches: The book splits the news feed at a high level into two flows. Feed publishing: when a user publishes a post, the post is written to cache and database, then pushed into friends' news feeds. Path: user (web/mobile) → load balancer → web servers → post service (stores the post in post cache + post DB), fanout service (pushes the post into friends' news feed cache), notification service (tells friends there's new content). News feed building: the feed is made by gathering friends' posts in reverse chronological order. Path: user → load balancer → web servers → news feed service → news feed cache (holds the post IDs that make up each feed). Splitting into flows is a reusable trick: most systems have a write path and a read path.
stages.interaction: Build-then-trace. (a) Two empty lanes labelled 'Publish a post' and 'Load my feed'. A palette of tiles (User, Load balancer, Web servers, Post service, Post cache, Post DB, Fanout service, News feed cache, Notification service, News feed service, plus 2 distractors: 'Search index', 'Payment service'). Learner taps tiles into each lane in path order; out-of-order or distractor taps shake. (b) Predict-then-watch: press 'Alice posts a photo' and first predict which box friends' feeds will read from later (Post DB / News feed cache (correct) / Notification service). Then animate a packet: through LB and web servers, splitting at the post service and fanout service, with 5 small packets flying to friends' feed-cache slots and a bell icon from the notification service. Then press 'Bob opens his feed' and the read packet goes LB → web servers → news feed service → news feed cache and returns a list of post IDs.
stages.check: Quiz: 'Which service puts a new post into friends' feeds?' Options: Notification service / Fanout service (correct) / Load balancer / News feed service.

stages.title: Pick the Zoom Level
stages.sub: API endpoints and schema: yes or no?
stages.teaches: Should step 2 include API endpoints and a database schema? The book says it depends on the problem. For a huge prompt like 'design Google search', that's too low-level for step 2. For a smaller one like a multiplayer poker game's backend, it's fair game. Talk to the interviewer about it. For the news feed, a couple of endpoints is a reasonable middle ground (Ch. 11 uses one to publish and one to retrieve the feed), with schema detail deferred.
stages.interaction: Zoom dial. Five prompt cards, each with a 3-position dial: 'Boxes only', 'Boxes + a few key APIs', 'Boxes + APIs + schema'. Learner sets the dial; the reveal explains. Answers: Design Google search → Boxes only; Multiplayer poker backend → Boxes + APIs + schema; News feed → Boxes + a few key APIs (e.g., publish post, get feed); URL shortener → Boxes + APIs + schema (small system, the API and the data model are the core); Design YouTube → Boxes only at first. Any answer that differs by one notch gets half credit plus the line 'when unsure, ask the interviewer'.
stages.check: Quiz: 'You're unsure whether to sketch the DB schema now. Best move?' Options: Always draw the full schema immediately / Never draw a schema in an interview / Ask the interviewer whether they'd like it now or later (correct) / Draw it secretly in the corner.

stages.title: Boss: Pushback at Minute 15
stages.teaches: Handling interviewer reactions in step 2 without stubbornness or over-engineering.
stages.interaction: Q.boss() with fixed choices: 'Adjust the blueprint', 'Defend with a reason', 'Park it for the deep dive', 'Ask a clarifying question'. Scenarios (answer, why): 1) 'Do we need a notification service at all?' → Defend with a reason (friends should hear about new posts; a short why, then move on). 2) 'Users mostly view on mobile with weak networks; video loads slowly.' → Adjust the blueprint (add CDN for media). 3) 'How exactly does fan-out handle a celebrity with millions of followers?' → Park it for the deep dive (acknowledge, note it, finish the blueprint first). 4) 'Make it faster.' → Ask a clarifying question (faster for posting or for loading the feed? which number?). 5) 'Your post service writes to the DB synchronously, then fans out synchronously. Posting feels slow.' → Adjust the blueprint (put fan-out behind a message queue so posting returns quickly). 6) 'Why a cache in front of the post DB?' → Defend with a reason (feeds are read far more than written; cache absorbs hot reads). Name: '🧱 The Whiteboard Wall'.
stages.check: Pass with at most 2 wrong; outro: 'Adjust when the point is valid, defend with a reason when it isn't, and park details until the deep dive.'

stages.title: Say It Like a Senior
stages.teaches: Narrating the diagram out loud, flow by flow.
stages.interaction: Q.drill(): prompt 'Scope is agreed. Walk the interviewer through your high-level news feed design.' Model answer (our words): 'I'll split it into two flows. Publishing: the client goes through a load balancer to stateless web servers. The post service saves the post to a database with a cache in front. A fanout service then pushes the post ID into each friend's feed in a news feed cache, and a notification service pings them. Reading: the client hits the news feed service, which reads the ready-made list of post IDs from the feed cache, newest first. Media goes to object storage and is served through a CDN. Before I go deeper, does this shape match what you want to focus on?'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: I split it into publish and read flows · I named the fanout service and the news feed cache · I mentioned load balancer and web servers · I ended by checking in with the interviewer.

caveats: The chapter's figures are deliberately high-level; how fan-out works (push on write vs pull on read, and the celebrity problem) is covered in Chapter 11. Here it's only previewed.
Object storage and CDN for video are our addition following the media requirement; the chapter's step 2 figures focus on the two flows.
Rough estimation in step 2 is optional; some interviewers skip it entirely, others insist. Ask first.

quests.d: Steps 3 and 4: pick the right components to deep-dive, avoid rabbit holes, and close strong
quests.goal: Your win today: choose and prioritise deep-dive topics with the interviewer, avoid low-signal rabbit holes, and deliver a wrap-up that names bottlenecks, failures, operations and the next scale step.
quests.bookSections: Step 3: Design deep dive (with the news feed deep-dive figures); Step 4: Wrap up

stages.title: Where to Dig
stages.teaches: Step 3 budget: 10–25 minutes. By now you should have agreed goals and scope, a blueprint, feedback on it, and a sense of which areas to focus on. Work with the interviewer to identify and prioritise components. Interviewers differ: some (especially for senior roles) want high-level talk about performance characteristics, bottlenecks and resource estimates; most want you to dig into a few components. The book's examples: for a URL shortener, the hash function that turns a long URL into a short one; for a chat system, how to cut latency and how to support online/offline status.
stages.interaction: Match prompts to dives. Six prompt cards (URL shortener, chat system, news feed, rate limiter, unique ID generator, web crawler) and a tray of deep-dive topics (hash function for short codes; latency + online presence; fan-out and feed retrieval; the limiting algorithm such as token bucket; ID bit layout; politeness and de-duplication). Learner drags each topic to its prompt. Only the first two pairs are from this chapter; others are flagged 'preview of later chapters'. After matching, a 'priority' mini-step: for the news feed, order three candidate topics by importance: fan-out on publish (1), feed retrieval path (2), UI pagination style (3).
stages.check: Quiz: 'For a chat system, which deep-dive focus does the book suggest?' Options: Choosing a font / Reducing latency and supporting online/offline status (correct) / The company logo / Unit test layout.

stages.title: The Rabbit-Hole Trap
stages.sub: Spend minutes where the signal is
stages.teaches: Time management matters in step 3: don't spend it on details that don't show you can design scalable systems. The book's example: explaining Facebook's feed ranking formula (EdgeRank) in depth eats time without showing scalability skill. Design the most critical components first. Signal per minute is the metric to optimise.
stages.interaction: Deep-dive planner. A 20-minute deep-dive bar and 6 topic tiles, each showing a minute cost; signal value is hidden until chosen. Tiles: 'Fan-out on write vs read for 5,000 friends' (6 min, high), 'Feed retrieval: cache layers and hydrating post IDs' (5 min, high), 'Handling a celebrity with millions of followers' (4 min, high), 'EdgeRank formula in detail' (8 min, low: trap), 'Which JSON library to use' (3 min, none), 'Media upload via object storage + CDN' (4 min, medium). Learner fills the bar; then 'Run the dive' animates a signal meter as each tile plays. Max score: the three high tiles plus media (19 min). Picking EdgeRank shows the interviewer glancing at the clock and a toast: 'interesting, but how does this scale?'
stages.check: Quiz: 'Why is a long EdgeRank explanation a poor use of deep-dive time?' Options: It's a secret / It shows little about scalable design while burning minutes (correct) / Ranking is never discussed in interviews / Interviewers don't know what it is.

stages.title: Peek at the Feed Deep Dive
stages.sub: A preview of fan-out (built in Ch. 11)
stages.teaches: The chapter's deep-dive figures expand the two flows: publishing (web servers, post service, fanout service, notification service, plus caches and DBs) and retrieval (news feed service reading feed cache then fetching post and user details). The key idea to preview: fan-out on write (push: when Alice posts, write her post ID into each friend's precomputed feed, fast reads, expensive for users with huge follower counts) vs fan-out on read (pull: build the feed when someone opens it, cheap writes, slower reads). With up to 5,000 friends, one post means up to 5,000 cache writes on push. Full treatment, including the hybrid used for celebrities, is in Chapter 11.
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch slider. A friend-count slider (10 → 5,000 → 'celebrity: 10M followers') and a toggle Push / Pull. The learner predicts, for each combo, whether the publish or the read will be slow (two buttons). Then animate: push with 5,000 friends shows 5,000 tiny writes streaming into feed-cache cells (fast publish counter at ~5,000 writes, instant read); push with 10M shows the write counter running for a long time with a 'hot key / backlog' warning; pull shows the publish as one write, and Bob's read pulling from many friends' post lists (read latency bar grows with friend count). Correct predictions: push → slow publish for celebrities, fast reads; pull → fast publish, slow reads.
stages.check: Quiz: 'With fan-out on write, which user makes publishing expensive?' Options: A user with 3 friends / A user with millions of followers (correct) / A user who never posts / A user on mobile.

stages.title: Land the Plane
stages.teaches: Step 4 budget: 3–5 minutes. The interviewer may ask follow-ups or let you choose what to add. Directions the book suggests: point out bottlenecks and possible improvements (never claim the design is perfect; there's always something to improve, and this shows critical thinking); give a short recap, especially if you discussed several options; error cases such as a server failing or network loss; operations: how you'd monitor metrics and error logs and roll the system out; the next scale step, e.g., what changes going from 1 million to 10 million users; other refinements you'd make with more time. And remember: the interview isn't over until the interviewer says it is.
stages.interaction: Closing-move picker. Timer shows 4:00 left. Eight closing cards; learner must pick exactly 3, then press 'Deliver'. Strong cards: 'Name the bottleneck: fan-out for celebrity accounts; propose a hybrid', 'What happens if the feed cache cluster loses a node: rebuild from the post DB and fall back to pull', 'How I'd monitor it: feed load latency, fan-out queue depth, error rates; roll out behind a flag', 'What breaks at 10× users: shard the post DB, add cache tiers'. Weak/trap cards: 'Say: I think the design is basically perfect', 'Re-explain every box from the start in detail', 'Ask: so... are we done?', 'Start a brand-new design for search'. Scoring: 3 strong = full XP; recap card is counted strong only if multiple options were discussed (show this rule in the reveal). Each trap picked costs a heart and shows why.
stages.check: Quiz: 'Interviewer: anything you'd improve?' Options: No, it's complete / Yes: the fan-out bottleneck for celebrities, plus monitoring and a plan for 10× growth (correct) / I'd rewrite it in another language / I'd need to check the book.

stages.title: Boss: Steps 3 & 4 Gauntlet
stages.sub: Dig, don't drown; close, don't coast
stages.teaches: Mixed decisions from the second half of the interview.
stages.interaction: Q.boss() with fixed choices: 'Go deeper here', 'Zoom out / move on', 'Ask the interviewer', 'Name a weakness'. Scenarios (answer, why): 1) Minute 24, you're 6 minutes into tuning a JSON parser → Zoom out / move on (low signal). 2) Interviewer: 'Tell me more about how fan-out handles celebrities.' → Go deeper here (they've signalled their priority). 3) You see two equally reasonable deep-dive targets and don't know which they care about → Ask the interviewer. 4) Minute 41, interviewer: 'Anything else?' → Name a weakness (bottleneck + improvement). 5) You've been explaining the ranking formula for 7 minutes → Zoom out / move on (rabbit hole). 6) Interviewer: 'What if a feed cache node dies?' → Go deeper here (failure handling is classic signal). 7) Wrap-up: you've covered fan-out but not operations → Name a weakness (say what you'd monitor and what's still fragile). Name: '🕳️ The Rabbit King'.
stages.check: Pass with at most 2 wrong; outro: 'Go deep where the interviewer points, name your weak spots before they do.'

stages.title: Say It Like a Senior
stages.teaches: A strong close is structured: weakness, failure, operations, next scale step.
stages.interaction: Q.drill(): prompt 'Four minutes left. The interviewer says: "Anything you'd add?"' Model answer (our words): 'A few things. The biggest bottleneck is fan-out for accounts with huge followings; I'd switch those to pull-on-read and keep push for everyone else. If a feed cache node fails, feeds can be rebuilt from the post store, with a pull-based fallback meanwhile. Operationally, I'd watch feed load latency, fan-out queue depth and error rates, and roll changes out gradually. At ten times the users I'd shard the post database and add more cache tiers. With more time I'd look at ranking and spam filtering.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: I named a bottleneck and a fix · I covered a failure case · I mentioned monitoring or rollout · I said what changes at the next scale step.

caveats: EdgeRank was Facebook's early, publicly described ranking formula; Facebook moved to machine-learned ranking years ago. The book uses it only as an example of a low-signal rabbit hole.
The push/pull fan-out comparison here is a preview; Chapter 11 covers it properly, including the hybrid approach and cache tiers.
Some interviewers deliberately steer the deep dive into areas you didn't plan; following their lead beats sticking to your plan.

quests.d: Full 45-minute mock interview of 'design a news feed', then switch seats and grade another candidate
quests.goal: Your win today: run a full 'design a news feed' interview through all four steps on the clock, choosing strong moves at each step, then judge another candidate's run as the interviewer would.
quests.bookSections: Whole chapter: the four steps, time allocation, the news feed example, dos and don'ts, red flags

stages.title: Step 1: Scope the Feed
stages.teaches: Applying step 1 under a clock: the same news feed facts as quest 3.2 (both platforms; publish + view friends' feed; reverse-chronological by assumption; up to 5,000 friends; 10M DAU; images and video), but now the learner must find them unprompted, with moves that cost time.
stages.interaction: Same layout as 0008: a sticky 45-minute clock bar with step label, a 'signal' meter, and an interviewer chat. Opening line from the interviewer: 'Design a news feed.' The learner gets a move menu each turn (4 options, mixed good/bad), e.g. 'Start drawing the architecture' (bad: interviewer interrupts, −signal, +2 min), 'Ask which features matter most' (good, reveals publish + view), 'Ask about scale now and in a year' (good, reveals 10M DAU), 'Ask about friend limits' (good, reveals 5,000), 'Ask whether posts have media' (good, reveals images + video), 'Ask mobile or web' (good), 'Ask about feed order' → interviewer says 'you decide' → follow-up menu where 'state reverse-chronological and write it down' is correct, 'assume silently' costs signal later, 'Ask about brand colours' (bad, −1 min, −signal), 'Ask about the existing stack' (good). Each good move costs 1 game-minute; each bad move 2–3 minutes. A requirements board fills as facts are revealed. Stage clears when all 6 facts are on the board; finishing within 10 minutes earns a bonus; past 10 minutes the interviewer nudges 'let's move on'.
stages.check: Q.quiz lock-in before moving on: 'Which assumption did you write down?' correct: reverse-chronological order (to keep v1 simple).

stages.title: Step 2: Sketch and Check In
stages.teaches: Applying step 2: the two flows, the box toolkit, and the check-in.
stages.interaction: Whiteboard SVG with two lanes (Publish, Read). Learner taps component tiles in whiteboard order; a component whose dependency isn't drawn yet costs a minute (e.g., Fanout service before Post service). Required: Publish lane = User → Load balancer → Web servers → Post service (+ post cache, post DB) → Fanout service → News feed cache, + Notification service; Read lane = User → Load balancer → Web servers → News feed service → News feed cache. Trap tiles (cost a heart, labelled as over-engineering by the interviewer): 'Blockchain post ledger', 'Custom consensus layer', 'ML ranking service (we agreed reverse-chron)'. Then a decision moment with 3 options: 'Keep going into details', 'Ask: does this shape work before I go deeper?' (correct, interviewer replies 'yes, and I'm curious about fan-out'), 'Declare the design complete'. Then an interviewer curveball: 'Where do the videos live?' → options: in the post DB as blobs / object storage + CDN (correct) / on the web servers' disks. The clock bar advances accordingly.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'The interviewer said they're curious about fan-out. What does that tell you about step 3?' correct: prioritise fan-out in the deep dive.

stages.title: Step 3: The Deep Dive
stages.teaches: Applying step 3: prioritise with the interviewer, avoid rabbit holes, ask for hints when stuck, think out loud.
stages.interaction: Three rounds, each a mini-scenario with 3–4 move options and time costs. Round A: pick a 15-minute plan from topic tiles (as in quest 3.4's planner) after the interviewer's hint: correct plans lead with fan-out, then feed retrieval; the EdgeRank tile is a trap that eats 8 minutes. Round B, 'Stuck moment': interviewer asks how to handle a user with 10M followers; options: 'Go silent and think' (−signal, +3 min), 'Think out loud: push is too costly here, maybe pull for celebrities; ask if they want me to explore a hybrid' (correct), 'Say it won't happen', 'Ask for a hint after sharing what you've tried' (also good, smaller signal). Round C, pushback: 'Why not just compute feeds on read for everyone?' options: 'Insist push is always better' (stubbornness flag), 'Agree instantly and redraw everything' (no reasoning), 'Compare: pull makes reads slow for users with many friends; I'd keep push for normal users and pull for celebrities' (correct). Signal meter and clock update after each round.
stages.check: Round results feed the scorecard; the stage clears when all three rounds are done.

stages.title: Switch Seats: Grade the Candidate
stages.teaches: Judging moves from the other side cements the dos, don'ts and red flags. A design can be technically fine and still get a no-hire if the process is poor.
stages.interaction: Mirror mode. A transcript of 'Candidate Riley' doing the same news feed prompt, ~14 lines covering all four steps with timestamps. The learner taps each line and tags it 'Strong signal', 'Red flag' or 'Neutral'. Lines include: 0:30 Riley starts drawing a load balancer immediately (red flag: no clarifying questions); 3:00 asks 'how many friends can a user have?' after being nudged (neutral/late); 9:00 draws publish and read flows clearly (strong); 12:00 never checks in, keeps going (red flag: no buy-in); 16:00 explains EdgeRank weights for 8 minutes (red flag: rabbit hole); 25:00 interviewer suggests pull for celebrities; Riley says push is always right and moves on (red flag: stubbornness); 30:00 proposes CDN for video with a clear reason (strong); 38:00 goes quiet for 3 minutes (red flag: thinking in silence); 41:00 'I think the design is complete, no real weaknesses' (red flag: never claim perfect); 43:00 asks 'is there anything you'd like me to go deeper on?' (strong). Then pick the overall decision: Strong hire / Hire / Lean no hire (correct: solid technical pieces, but skipped scoping, no buy-in, stubbornness and the 'perfect' close are serious process flags) / Strong no hire. Reveal shows which book rule each red flag broke.
stages.check: Pass if at least 10 of the lines are tagged correctly and the decision is 'Lean no hire'; otherwise show the correct tags and allow a retry.

stages.title: Step 4: Wrap It Up
stages.teaches: Applying step 4: bottlenecks, failure cases, operations, next scale curve, recap if useful; don't end before the interviewer does.
stages.interaction: Pick exactly 3 of 8 closing cards (same card set as quest 3.4's 'Land the Plane' but shuffled, with the wording varied), then 'Deliver my close'. The interviewer reacts per card. After delivery, a final beat: interviewer says 'Thanks, that's all from me. Any questions?' with options: 'Ask for feedback or ask about the team's real challenges' (good) vs 'No, bye' (neutral) vs 'So did I pass?' (weak). The clock bar should finish near 45:00; overruns cost signal.
stages.check: Stage clears on delivery; score feeds the final scorecard.

stages.title: Say It Like a Senior + Scorecard
stages.sub: The 60-second game plan, then your verdict
stages.teaches: A compressed, spoken run-through of the whole interview for the news feed, plus a scorecard that maps the run to the five signals from quest 3.1.
stages.interaction: Q.drill(): prompt 'Give the 60-second version of how you ran this interview, step by step.' Model answer (our words): 'I started by scoping: mobile and web, posting and viewing friends' posts, newest first by assumption, up to 5,000 friends, 10 million daily users, images and video. Then I sketched two flows: publishing through the post service and a fanout service into a feed cache, and reading from the news feed service out of that cache, with media on a CDN, and checked the shape with the interviewer. In the deep dive I focused on fan-out, push for normal users and pull for celebrities, and on the retrieval path. I closed by naming the celebrity bottleneck, cache failure recovery, the metrics I'd watch, and what changes at ten times the scale.' After the drill, render a scorecard: five signal bars (Design skill, Collaboration, Under pressure, Ambiguity, Good questions) computed from choices across stages 1–5, total game-minutes used vs 45, red flags triggered (listed by name), and a verdict: Strong hire / Hire / Lean hire / Lean no hire. Store it under a separate localStorage key `sdq:v1:<lesson-id>-interview` (like 0008), wrapped in try/catch.
stages.check: Self-grade checks: I covered all four steps in order · I quoted the key scope numbers (5,000 friends, 10M DAU) · I named both flows and the fan-out trade-off · I closed with a bottleneck and an operations point.

caveats: The 45-minute game clock and per-move minute costs are our own game framing; the book gives ranges per step, not a scoring system.
Hire/no-hire verdicts here are a teaching device. Real decisions combine several interviews and company-specific rubrics; a single process slip rarely sinks a strong candidate on its own.
The fan-out details (hybrid push/pull, CDN for media) go beyond Chapter 3 and follow Chapter 11 and common practice.
Interviewers vary: some drive the deep dive themselves, some let you choose. The strong move is always to read their cues and check in.

cheatsheetOutline: One page, 'The Interview Arena' (Ch. 3). Header: the four-step timeline bar with minute ranges for a 45-minute session (scope 3–10, high-level 10–15, deep dive 10–25, wrap-up 3–5) and a note that the ranges flex. Section 3.1 Rules of the Room: what's graded (design skill, collaboration, pressure, ambiguity, good questions); the three red flags (over-engineering, narrow-mindedness, stubbornness) each with a one-line example; Dos vs Don'ts as two short columns. Section 3.2 Ask Before You Build: four question families (features, users, growth at 3/6/12 months, existing stack); 'answer or assume, then write it down'; the news feed scope card (mobile + web; publish + view; reverse-chron by assumption; 5,000 friends; 10M DAU; images + video) with the implication of each. Section 3.3 Blueprint & Buy-in: box toolkit list; the two-flow diagram (publish: LB → web servers → post service + post cache/DB → fanout service → news feed cache, + notification; read: LB → web servers → news feed service → news feed cache); zoom-level rule for APIs/schema (Google search: no; poker backend: yes; ask). Section 3.4 Dive Deep, Land Clean: deep-dive examples (URL shortener → hash function; chat → latency + presence; news feed → fan-out); rabbit-hole warning (EdgeRank); push vs pull fan-out mini-table (preview of Ch. 11); wrap-up checklist (bottleneck + improvement, recap, failure cases, monitoring/logs/rollout, next scale step 1M→10M, never 'perfect'). BOSS Run the Room: the 60-second game plan script and the scorecard's five signals. Footer: honest caveats (ranges are a guide; many loops are 60 min; requirements lists and estimation expectations vary; news feed numbers are illustrative).
